newsitem.title: FRANCE: France shuts down land-based nuclear missiles.
newsitem.headline: France shuts down land-based nuclear missiles.

text.p: France shuts down land-based nuclear missiles on Monday when it ends a 25-year doomsday watch at an underground launch base as part of defence cuts ordered by President Jacques Chirac.
The 18 S3D missiles, poised for launch from silos buried beneath scenic Provence countryside in southeastern France, will be deactivated early on Monday.

Two pairs of officers, in separate bunkers 40 km (25 miles) apart, will hand back keys and launch codes that would have enabled them to fire the missiles, each with a one megatonne warhead, in a direct link-up with Chirac.

The formal end of the operational alert will be announced on Monday afternoon in a ceremony at Saint-Christol, headquarters of the First Group of Strategic Missiles, attended by air force chief of staff General Jean Rannou.
"Monday at zero hours, the operational mission will be stopped. We will not be able to fire any longer," General Claude Bigot, commander of the First Group of Strategic Missiles, told Reuters.

Bigot will hand over official command on Monday to an air force colonel who will be in charge of dismantling the missiles, which have a range of 3,500 km (2,200 miles), far enough to strike Moscow and beyond in what was the Soviet Union.

From Monday, France's nuclear defences will be assured by nuclear weapons aboard submarines and bombers. Chirac has already decided to dismantle short-range Hades nuclear missiles in a restructuring after the Cold War.
The Plateau d'Albion site covers 800 sq km (310 sq miles). Dismantling the weapons will take 30 months and cost slightly less than 400 million francs ($77.5 million).
The missiles have been in place since 1971, a symbol of the independence of France's nuclear strike force.

Chirac decided last year to close the site, but the news was overshadowed by his simultaneous announcement France was resuming nuclear tests in French Polynesia in the South Pacific. The six tests ended in January after a torrent of criticism.
By coincidence, the closure of the Plateau d'Albion coincides with a visit to Paris by Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer on Monday to repair ties strained by the nuclear row.
Officers will continue to watch Plateau d'Albion from the underground command posts to ensure nuclear safety until all the missiles are dismantled.
Defence Minister Charles Millon has promised to maintain the number of jobs. The current garrison of 1,166 brings the surrounding region an estimated one million francs a day.

One possibility is to turn the site into a training centre for pilots of the Franco-German Tiger combat helicopter. Some local residents are reluctant to swap silent, unlaunched nuclear missiles for noisy helicopters, however. (1=5.163 French Franc)
